title: TCP U1·W1 — Individual Tax Planning & Gross Income (2026)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — planning, not just filing

The Tax Compliance and Planning (TCP) discipline goes beyond REG's rule-stating into planning — structuring transactions and timing to minimize tax within the law. It starts where every individual return starts: the individual tax formula and what counts as gross income. For MBG's owner, Jordan Reed, the difference between a good and a poor outcome is often when income is recognized and which exclusions apply. All figures use the 2026 Public Law 119-21 baseline.

The individual tax formula

Every plan works within one structure. Gross income minus above-the-line adjustments equals adjusted gross income (AGI); AGI minus the greater of the standard or itemized deduction, and minus the qualified business income (QBI) deduction, equals taxable income; the tax is computed on taxable income, then reduced by credits and increased by other taxes (self-employment, net investment income, AMT). Note a 2026 anchor: the personal exemption is permanently $0 (§70103), so AGI and the deduction choice carry the weight that exemptions once did. AGI is the pivotal number because many deductions, credits, and phaseouts key off it — lowering AGI is a recurring planning lever.

Filing status and rate structure

Filing status — single, married filing jointly (MFJ), married filing separately (MFS), head of household (HOH), qualifying surviving spouse — sets the rate brackets, the standard deduction, and many phaseout thresholds. Choosing correctly is itself planning: HOH (an unmarried taxpayer maintaining a home for a qualifying person) is far more favorable than single, and MFJ versus MFS can swing a couple's liability. The progressive brackets mean planning often aims to smooth income across years to avoid spiking into a higher marginal rate.

Gross income — inclusions

Gross income is "all income from whatever source derived" unless excluded. Inclusions span wages, interest, dividends (with qualified dividends taxed at the lower capital-gains rates), business income, capital gains, rents and royalties, retirement distributions, and the taxable portion of Social Security. Timing matters: a cash-basis individual recognizes income when received (or constructively received), so deferring a year-end bonus or billing into January can shift income to the next year. Alimony from agreements after 2018 is not income to the recipient (and not deductible by the payer) — a frequently tested change.

Gross income — exclusions

Several receipts are excluded from gross income, and steering income into excluded forms is core planning. Key exclusions: gifts and inheritances (taxed, if at all, under the transfer-tax system, not income tax), municipal-bond interest, life-insurance proceeds paid at death, gain on the sale of a principal residence up to $250,000/$500,000 (§121), qualified scholarships, and many employer-provided fringe benefits (health coverage, up to limits on others). The exclusion for discharge of qualified principal-residence debt applies only to discharges completed by the end of 2025, so it is generally unavailable in 2026 — a baseline detail the exam tests.

Above-the-line adjustments

Adjustments (deductions "above the line") reduce AGI directly and are available even to taxpayers who take the standard deduction — making them especially valuable. They include the educator expense deduction (retained even as misc 2% deductions were terminated), health savings account (HSA) contributions, the deductible half of self-employment tax and the SE health-insurance deduction, traditional IRA contributions (subject to limits), and student-loan interest (phased out by income). Because these lower AGI, they also relax AGI-based phaseouts elsewhere — a double benefit a planner exploits first.

Timing strategies

The planner's primary tools are timing and character. Deferring income to a later year (postponing a bonus, using installment sales, contributing to retirement plans) delays the tax and can keep a taxpayer in a lower bracket; accelerating deductions into the current year does the reverse. The aim is to manage the marginal rate across years — accelerate income into a low-rate year, defer it from a high-rate year. For a business owner like Jordan Reed, whose income varies with the construction cycle, this multi-year smoothing is often worth more than any single deduction.

The standard deduction decision

Finally, every individual chooses the greater of the standard deduction (a fixed amount by filing status, enhanced and made permanent under the 2026 baseline) or itemized deductions (next week's topic). Because itemizing only helps when itemized deductions exceed the standard amount, a common strategy is bunching — concentrating deductible payments (charitable gifts, elective medical) into one year to clear the standard-deduction threshold, then taking the standard deduction the next. The choice is recomputed every year as circumstances change, and it frames the deduction planning that follows.

Constructive receipt and assignment of income

Two doctrines constrain timing plans. Constructive receipt means a cash-basis taxpayer is taxed when income is made available without restriction — you cannot defer a December paycheck merely by leaving it uncashed, because it was available. Assignment of income means income is taxed to the person who earns it (or owns the income-producing property); a taxpayer cannot shift earned income to a lower-bracket family member by directing the payment elsewhere. Together they set the boundary of legitimate timing: defer income that is genuinely not yet available, and shift income only by transferring the underlying asset, not just the cash stream.

Dependents and the kiddie tax

Income-shifting to children has a limit: the kiddie tax taxes a child's unearned income above a small threshold at the parents' marginal rate, neutralizing the benefit of putting investment assets in a young child's name. Dependents still matter for filing status, the child tax credit, and education benefits, so identifying who qualifies is itself part of the plan. The lesson is that income-shifting to family works mainly through earned income — employing a child in the business at a reasonable wage — rather than gifted investments, which the kiddie tax and assignment-of-income doctrine neutralize.

CMA bridge

For Jordan Reed as MBG's owner, individual tax planning is inseparable from the business: when to take a bonus versus leave earnings in the entity, how to time income against a variable construction cycle, and which fringe benefits to route through the company. The CFO who understands the individual formula can structure the owner's compensation to minimize the combined entity-and-individual tax — the planning mindset TCP develops.

Practice and recap

  1. Apply the individual formula: gross income − adjustments = AGI − greater(standard, itemized) − QBI = taxable income → tax − credits + other taxes (personal exemption = $0 in 2026).
  2. Choose filing status strategically (HOH vs single; MFJ vs MFS) — it sets brackets, the standard deduction, and phaseouts.
  3. Identify gross-income inclusions (wages/interest/qualified dividends/business/gains; post-2018 alimony excluded) and exclusions (gifts/inheritances, municipal interest, life insurance, §121, scholarships, fringe benefits).
  4. Use above-the-line adjustments to cut AGI, and time income/deductions to manage the marginal rate; decide standard vs itemized (bunching).

Recap: individual tax planning works within the formula — gross income less above-the-line adjustments yields the pivotal AGI, then the greater of the standard or itemized deduction and the QBI deduction yield taxable income (with the personal exemption permanently $0 in 2026); gross income includes wages, interest, qualified dividends, business income, and gains while excluding gifts/inheritances, municipal interest, life-insurance proceeds, §121 home gain, scholarships, and many fringe benefits; and the planner's levers are reducing AGI through adjustments and managing the marginal rate by timing income and deductions and bunching to beat the standard deduction.

questions.q: Under the 2026 baseline, the personal exemption amount is:
questions.explain: PL 119-21 §70103 makes the personal exemption permanently $0.

questions.q: Adjusted gross income (AGI) is pivotal because:
choices: Many deductions, credits, and phaseouts key off it
questions.explain: AGI drives numerous AGI-based limits, so lowering it is a core planning lever.

questions.q: Alimony paid under a 2020 divorce agreement is:
choices: Not income to the recipient and not deductible by the payer
Income to the recipient and deductible by the payer
questions.explain: For agreements after 2018, alimony is neither deductible nor includible in income.

questions.q: Which item is EXCLUDED from gross income?
questions.explain: Life-insurance death proceeds are excluded; the others are included.

questions.q: An above-the-line adjustment is valuable because it:
choices: Reduces AGI even if the taxpayer takes the standard deduction
questions.explain: Adjustments reduce AGI directly and are available regardless of standard vs itemized.

questions.q: A taxpayer expecting a higher tax bracket next year should generally:
questions.explain: Accelerate income into the lower-rate year and defer deductions to the higher-rate year.

choices: Exceed the standard deduction in one year, then take the standard deduction the next
questions.explain: Concentrating deductible payments into one year clears the standard-deduction threshold for that year.
